summary: A 1975 note examining how much of the response time in debugging programs across the network comes from ARPANET communication itself.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 685 reports measurements from a debugger that used a PDP-10 at BBN and a PDP-11 running the program. The distant test's average wait per message was slightly longer than the local test's.

questions: how long does cross network debugging take
how long did cross-network debugging take
subtitle: Measurements of the extra wait when a debugger communicates across the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: A debugger split across computers depends on network replies, so the network's contribution to the user's waiting time needed measurement.
tldr.mechanism: The report compares a standard X-NET debugging session at BBN with one reaching SRI-ARC, using 35 active commands in each scenario.
tldr.outcome: The measured mean wait per message was 1.75 seconds locally and 1.89 seconds at the distant site. The author concludes that cross-network debugging was practical in this test.

today: RFC 685 is a report of an X-NET debugging measurement conducted in 1975. It records the authors' conclusion that cross-network debugging was practical in that test.

sections.title: A Debugger Split Across Two Computers
sections.content:
The X-NET debugger at BBN used a PDP-10 for complex debugging work and sent simpler operations to a PDP-11 where the program ran. Those operations included examining and changing memory, starting and stopping execution, and setting breakpoints.

The report asks how much network communication added to response time. It compares a local PDP-11 at BBN with a PDP-11 at SRI-ARC in California, reached through at least nine IMPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The debugger did some work locally and sent other commands to the computer running the program. The test compared a nearby computer with one across the network.

sections.title: The Measurement
sections.content:
Each session lasted about 10 minutes and followed the same scenario of 35 active commands. The commands included loading a program, examining memory, setting a breakpoint, and starting or stopping execution.

The report defines wait as elapsed time from handing a message to the network routines through receipt of the reply. It measured waits and transferred bytes both per message and per active command.
sections.plainLanguage: The same 35-command debugging task ran at each site. The measurement included the time from sending a command until its reply returned.

sections.title: Results and Conclusion
sections.content:
Average wait per message was 1.75 seconds for the local BBN session and 1.89 seconds for the distant SRI-ARC session. The report notes that the variation was large, partly because the sample was small and commands differed in size and complexity.

The author concludes that the network delay was tolerable and of the same order as delays on moderately loaded time-sharing systems. The report does not break the delay into separate causes.
sections.plainLanguage: The distant session had a somewhat longer average wait than the local session. The author judged the measured delay tolerable, while noting the test could not explain each source of delay.
